name: Optro
tagline: AI-assisted workflow software for audit, risk and compliance teams.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Products in this space are almost always quoted per engagement or per firm, not listed publicly.

verdictSummary: The software here is the thin part: forms, a control register, evidence attachments, workflow states, a report generator. What buyers are actually paying for is the encoded methodology, the mapping to specific frameworks and standards, and the fact that a reviewer or regulator will accept the resulting workpapers. An agent can absolutely build you a risk register with evidence tracking and AI-drafted findings in a weekend, and it will look convincing. It will not carry an opinion, a sign-off trail anyone trusts, or the framework mappings maintained by people who read the standards updates for a living. If you are one person tracking your own controls, build it. If anything downstream depends on someone else believing the output, do not.
coreLoopDIY: A local risk and control register where you log controls, attach evidence files, walk each one through a test/review workflow, and export a dated findings report with AI-drafted summaries.
requirements: An LLM API key in .env if you want drafted findings text
Somewhere durable to keep the SQLite file and evidence folder, because losing your audit trail defeats the point
whatYouLose: Maintained framework mappings, so when a standard or control catalog changes, that is now your reading assignment
Any credibility with an external reviewer, client, or regulator who wants to know who signed off and on what basis
Methodology: the built-in question sets and test procedures that tell a non-expert what evidence is even sufficient
Immutable audit logging, retention controls and access separation, which are usually the reason this category is bought at all
Multi-reviewer workflow, so preparer/reviewer separation becomes you promising yourself you were careful
moatNotes: The defensible asset is the methodology library plus the mapping maintenance, not the CRUD around it. Second is the signature: someone external has to accept the workpaper.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because in audit and compliance, the artifact is only worth what the reader believes about how it was produced. Teams buy this software to inherit a defensible process: standard test procedures, framework mappings kept current by someone else, tamper-evident logs, and preparer/reviewer separation that survives a question six quarters later. A homegrown tracker gives you the same tables and none of that. The cost of being wrong is a qualified opinion, a failed certification, or a client walking, which makes a per-seat license look extremely cheap.
notes: The register is a weekend; the methodology and the sign-off are not. The moat is maintained framework mappings plus the fact that someone external has to accept the workpaper, and they accept it because of whose process made it.
prompt:
Build a local-first risk and control register for one person, no cloud, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions: Next.js 15 with the App Router, TypeScript, SQLite via better-sqlite3, Tailwind for styling. Everything runs with `npm run dev` on localhost. Store the DB at ./data/registry.db and uploaded evidence as files under ./data/evidence/, both gitignored.

Data model:
- Framework: name, version, notes. Seeded empty, I add my own.
- Control: framework_id, reference code, title, description, owner, frequency (annual, quarterly, monthly, continuous), status (not_started, in_progress, tested, exception, remediated).
- Test: control_id, tested_on date, tester name, procedure text, result (pass, fail, partial), notes.
- Evidence: test_id, original filename, stored path, sha256 hash, uploaded_at.
- AuditLog: append-only table, one row per create/update/delete with timestamp, table, row id, and a JSON diff. Never allow updates or deletes on this table in code.

UI, four pages:
1. Dashboard: counts by status, a list of controls overdue based on frequency and last test date.
2. Controls list with filters by framework, status, owner. Inline edit.
3. Control detail: description, test history, add a test, drag-drop evidence files. Show each file's sha256 and let me re-verify a stored file against its recorded hash.
4. Report: pick a framework and a date range, render a printable HTML page of controls, latest test result, exceptions, and evidence filenames with hashes. Include a footer with generation timestamp and a hand-typed preparer name.

Optional AI, off unless OPENAI_API_KEY is set in .env: one button on the control detail page that drafts a findings paragraph from the test notes. It writes into an editable textarea, never saves directly, and the saved record marks whether text was AI-drafted.

Explicitly out of scope: multi-user auth, preparer/reviewer approval chains, prebuilt framework content of any kind, e-signatures, integrations with ticketing or cloud providers, anything claiming a control is compliant. The app records what I tested and when. It does not judge.

Include a seed script with three fake controls so the UI is not empty, and a README with a blunt limitations section stating this is a personal tracker and not audit evidence for any third party.
